title: Making Policy in the Exectuive Branch: Money, Expertise, Issue Framing, and Public Pressure
text:
The Environmental Justice Frame

What is environmental justice, and why does the Biden administration require 40% of federal spending to be spent in environmental justice communities?
The EJ movement began in local resistance to toxic waste in places like the Alt-geld Gardens housing complex on Chicago’s South Side, where activists like Hazel Johnson had been organizing tenants years before a young Barak Obama showed up in 1984. Surrounded by manufacturing and toxic waste dumps, this neighborhood got the nickname “the toxic doughnut.”
Dorceta Taylor describes how black-led campaigns like Johnson’s fused with the American Indian Movement, Chicano, and farmworker movements and drew on civil rights and union organizing to push the environmental justice frame onto the national policy agenda.
Began appearing in federal policy documents in the 1980s
I aim to add more systematic quantitative data on the broad trends regarding the influence of the EJ movement on the federal policy agenda that Taylor and others have mapped.

Why does this matter?

“Environmental” policy debates are rarely about distributions of costs and benefits

Reframing policy in distributive justice terms can shape normative, political, and economic analysis.

For this research: “environmental justice” is a distinct phrase (few false positives) without many synonyms (few false negatives)


Scholars of bureaucracy focus on technical information


Bureaucratic policymaking, especially, is about expertise (Wagner 2010)

Everything we know about lobbying, especially lobbying in agency rulemaking, tells us that information is the currency of lobbying.
Information causes policymakers to change their minds, especially when policymakers are experts and lawyers.
Indeed, research, including my own research elsewhere, shows that business groups dominate lobbying in rulemaking because they can generate and provide relevant information.
Thus far, by “information,” scholars generally mean technical and legal information.

How might political information matter?

Advancing frames about who is affected/deserving?
Novelty vs. legibility?
Pressure:

Coalition size? (Dwidar 2021, Nelson & Yackee 2012)
Public attention?

Citing limits on unequal harms
The Biden EPA addressed EJ complaints that emissions trading could lead to pollution hot spots but asserted that the policy included backstops intended to limit inequalities:

The EPA is cognizant of these concerns and believes that emission trading and averaging are not necessarily incompatible with environmental justice. The EPA is including limitations on the use of compliance flexibilities in state plans that should help address these EJ concerns.

text:
Failing to respond
Example: the Obama Nuclear Regulatory Commission claimed to have received no input on environmental justice comments on Emergency Preparedness Regulations NRC-2008-0122.

The NRC requested public comments on any environmental justice considerations that may be related to this rule and no comments were received.

This was incorrect. A comment from Hudson River Sloop Clearwater, Inc. raised serious EJ concerns that went unaddressed in the rule:

The rules and guidance are based on a fantasy world in which the terrain around nuclear power stations is perfectly flat, radiation plumes do not move up and down, the wind blows at the same speed in a constant direction throughout an accident, and most people follow the instructions they are given about the need to evacuate.


Need for Site-Specific Analysis of Transport-Dependent Populations: The present guidance suggests that because 50% of residents would offer rides to those in need, approximately 50% of the transit-dependent population in the EPZ would rideshare. Criteria for Development of ETE Studies (April 23, 2009) at 13. This assumption fails to account for the likely separation of transit-dependent environmental justice populations from more affluent populations. Furthermore, it takes no account of attitudes towards race and the potential reluctance of whites to offer rides to African- Americans. Instead of presuming that 50% of the transit-dependent population will rideshare, the presumption should be that only a small percentage will rideshare unless the licensee can show that there are no geographical concentrations of transit-dependent populations and that there is no racial or sociological bias with regard to ridesharing.


…people would be foolish to follow the directions of first responders if they are based on totally unrealistic modeling. Indeed, it is doubtful whether people would follow instructions even if they were based on the best predictions possible. The experiences during Hurricane Katrina also underline that it is even more doubtful whether the response planned for environmental justice communities would actually materialize.

section: Modeling the probability of policy change
text:
Modeling the probability of policy change
(1) Variation across agencies:
Pr(Policy Change | President) ~ Policy Demands + Coalition Size + Public Attention + Agency’s Prior Rate of Addressing Environmental Justice (+ Interactions)
(2) Variation within agencies:
Pr(Policy Change | President & Agency) ~ Policy Demands + Coalition Size + Public Attention (+ Interactions)

Both of my DVs—adding EJ language and changing existing EJ language–are dichotomous, so I’m going to use logit regression.
The main models use president and agency fixed effects, so I’m focusing on variation within presidential administrations and within the agency, but I also assess differences across presidents and agencies by estimating the same models with indicators rather than fixed effects.
Because log odds coefficients are hard to interpret and because my models have interactions, I am going to skip the regression table and just show you predicted probabilities.


(1.1a) Logit: \(Y_i = \beta_{1:n} X_{i} + \delta_p + \epsilon_{ip}\)
\(Y_i\): the log odds of change in rule \(i\) by agency \(k\) under president \(p\) 
\(X_{i}\): features of rule \(i\) - whether comments raise environmental justice

agency \(k\)’s share of prior draft rules mentioning environmental justice
the number of organizations raising environmental justice (logged)
the total number of comments (logged) \(\times\) whether comments raise environmental justice

\(\delta_p\): president fixed effects
\(\epsilon_{ip}\): cluster-robust errors by president

Heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors (White correction), where it is assumed that the errors are independent, but the variance of their generative law may vary.
If vcov = “cluster”, then the arbitrary correlation of the errors within clusters is accounted for. Same for vcov = “twoway”: arbitrary correlation within each of the two clusters is accounted for. fixest: sandwich
same as xtreg cluster in stata


(1.1b) Logit: \(Y_i = \beta_{1:n} X_{i} + \gamma_k + \delta_p + \epsilon_{ipk}\)
\(Y_i\): the log odds of change in rule \(i\) by agency \(k\) under president \(p\) 
\(X_{i}\): features of rule \(i\) - whether comments raise environmental justice - the number of organizations raising environmental justice (logged) - the total number of comments (logged) \(\times\) whether comments raise environmental justice
\(\gamma_k + \delta_p\): president & agency fixed effects
\(\epsilon_{ipk}\): cluster-robust errors by president & agency

Because I expect decreasing marginal effects of additional comments, both overall (i.e., public attention) and those that mention EJ (coalition size), I use logged values.
However, the conclusions are largely the same if I use a quadratic function instead. That analysis suggests that medium levels of attention are not so impactful. A small level of attention matters, and then it takes a very large amount of additional pressure to move things, which makes sense. For hypothesis testing, however, all of the effects are in the same direction, so I am going to present predicted probabilities from these models here.

The Environmental Justice Frame

What is environmental justice, and why does the Biden administration require 40% of federal spending to be spent in environmental justice communities?
The EJ movement began in local resistance to toxic waste in places like the Alt-geld Gardens housing complex on Chicago’s South Side, where activists like Hazel Johnson had been organizing tenants years before a young Barak Obama showed up in 1984. Surrounded by manufacturing and toxic waste dumps, this neighborhood got the nickname “the toxic doughnut.”
Dorceta Taylor describes how black-led campaigns like Johnson’s fused with the American Indian Movement, Chicano, and farmworker movements and drew on civil rights and union organizing to push the environmental justice frame onto the national policy agenda.
Began appearing in federal policy documents in the 1980s
I aim to add more systematic quantitative data on the broad trends regarding the influence of the EJ movement on the federal policy agenda that Taylor and others have mapped.

Why does this matter?

“Environmental” policy debates are rarely about distributions of costs and benefits

Reframing policy in distributive justice terms can shape normative, political, and economic analysis.

For this research: “environmental justice” is a distinct phrase (few false positives) without many synonyms (few false negatives)

Example: the Obama Nuclear Regulatory Commission claimed to have received no input on environmental justice comments on Emergency Preparedness Regulations NRC-2008-0122.

The NRC requested public comments on any environmental justice considerations that may be related to this rule and no comments were received.

This was incorrect. A comment from Hudson River Sloop Clearwater, Inc. raised serious EJ concerns that went unaddressed in the rule:

The rules and guidance are based on a fantasy world in which the terrain around nuclear power stations is perfectly flat, radiation plumes do not move up and down, the wind blows at the same speed in a constant direction throughout an accident, and most people follow the instructions they are given about the need to evacuate.


Need for Site-Specific Analysis of Transport-Dependent Populations: The present guidance suggests that because 50% of residents would offer rides to those in need, approximately 50% of the transit-dependent population in the EPZ would rideshare. Criteria for Development of ETE Studies (April 23, 2009) at 13. This assumption fails to account for the likely separation of transit-dependent environmental justice populations from more affluent populations. Furthermore, it takes no account of attitudes towards race and the potential reluctance of whites to offer rides to African-Americans. Instead of presuming that 50% of the transit-dependent population will rideshare, the presumption should be that only a small percentage will rideshare unless the licensee can show that there are no geographical concentrations of transit-dependent populations and that there is no racial or sociological bias with regard to ridesharing.


…people would be foolish to follow the directions of first responders if they are based on totally unrealistic modeling. Indeed, it is doubtful whether people would follow instructions even if they were based on the best predictions possible. The experiences during Hurricane Katrina also underline that it is even more doubtful whether the response planned for environmental justice communities would actually materialize.

title: Notes on “Patrons, Citizens, and the Locus of Organizational Bias”
text:
The contribution
This paper beautifully captures the organization of bias AND the bias of organization.
I would emphasize the contribution of the benchmark model. There are really two important contributions: (1) the benchmark model (without patrons) + (2) the model with patrons.
Consider “The Organization of Bias and How Patrons Bias Organization” as a title.

title: Notes on “Patrons, Citizens, and the Locus of Organizational Bias”
section: 1. Model inequality in resources and political efficacy
text:
1. Model inequality in resources and political efficacy
While true that the upper-class accent may be the signature of one-sided patrons “instead” of the voice of an already advantaged public (p. 29), your model easily extends to both.
The same membership fee may be easier for some people to pay than others; this increases their \(c\).
Political efficacy makes some people more likely to be type H than L.
Both of these may be correlated with \(y\), likely reinforcing the asymmetry of patrons.

title: Notes on “Patrons, Citizens, and the Locus of Organizational Bias”
text:
2. Model repression
The patron model is a subsidy model. The mirror is one where some exogenous force imposes costs on group entry or citizen joining — for example, government repression, social stigma, scapegoating, or attacks from other groups.
Repression that affects group entry increases \(k\) (or is added to \(k\) if it is helpful to distinguish operating costs from repression costs).
Repression that affects joining (e.g., stigma) increases \(c\) (or is added to \(c\) if it is helpful to distinguish membership fees from social sanctions)
Both of these may be correlated with \(y\).

title: Notes on “Patrons, Citizens, and the Locus of Organizational Bias”
section: 3. Endogenize citizen ideology & engagement to group density in \(t-1\)
text:
3. Endogenize citizen ideology & engagement to group density in \(t-1\)

The current model captures the organization of existing biases in preferences and engagement.
Endogenizing both would capture the persuasion and mobilization functions of groups
With patrons, the dynamic game would show how patrons move public opinion and organize new constituencies into politics over time.


[Politics is] a field of action that is, at once, practically bounded and potentially infinite… Unless we consider the changing and polysemous reality of meaning, social scientists run the risk of treating values and attitudes as antecedent, given and fixed. (Woodly 2015, p. 211)

title: Notes on “Patrons, Citizens, and the Locus of Organizational Bias”
text:
4. Dynamics with startup costs
\(k\) is defined as operating costs. What about startup costs?
If it is cheaper for groups to enter if they entered in \(t-1\) (it’s easier to maintain a group than start one), then changes in \(y\) will cause only a lagged response in active support.
In the benchmark model, group voice would lag citizen preferences, potentially forever. For simplicity, I think you would just need to show two states of \(y\) and three time periods, where a shift to some \(y'\) in \(t_2\) fails to achieve the same active support in \(t_3\) with this modification and thus will never do so.
Patron bias would compound over time and persist after patrons exit.

title: Notes on “Patrons, Citizens, and the Locus of Organizational Bias”
text:
5. Dynamics with sticky identities
Related to #4 and #5, it may also be costly for people in some regions of \(y\) to switch from L to H, but once they do, it persists.

“The original show was fighting for tolerance. Our fight is for acceptance.” - Tan France, Queer Eye

If \(u_i\) in \(t\) is affected by whether \(i\) had group support in \(t-1\) (they had an identity group), then changes in \(y\) will cause incomplete responses in active support.
In the benchmark model, the dead hand of the past would exert a conservative force on group voice via available/mobilized identities (regions of \(y\) where engagement is normal or even just conceivable). Again, I think you would just need to show two states of \(y\) and three time periods, where a shift to some \(y'\) in \(t_2\) fails to achieve the same active support in \(t_3\) with this modification and thus will never do so.
Again, patron bias would compound over time and persist after patrons exit due to the identity groups they helped to form/activate.

title: Notes on “Patrons, Citizens, and the Locus of Organizational Bias”
text:
6 Model re-framing/realignment
Consider a two dimension space \(y\) and \(z\), with each individual \(i\) at \((y_i, z_i)\)). Set patrons and endogeneity aside for a second, and model each alternative dimension of conflict as in the benchmark model. At entry, groups must decide which frame to adopt. They can locate only at \((x_j, 0)\) or \((0, x_j')\). The dimension with fewer groups at 0 defines the conflict. This may be hard to solve. Perhaps it gets easier to solve with patrons subsidizing entry on one dimension. Perhaps not. But, intuitively, patrons may also affect the conflict chosen.

Political conflict is not like an intercollegiate debate in which the opponents agree in advance on a definition of the issues. As a matter of fact, the definition of the alternatives is the supreme instrument of power; antagonists can rarely agree on what the issues are because power is involved in the definition.


He who determines what politics is about runs the country, because the definition of alternatives is the choice of conflicts, and the choice of conflicts allocates power. – E. E. Schattschneider

Social movement literature
There is a lot of adjacent social movement scholarship, mostly in sociology, that may suggest further interpretations or extensions.
For example, the debate around resource mobilization theory vs. identity work and persuasion inspired some of my suggestions above.
Also see Forester on how groups affect preferences and Carpenter’s “Agenda Democracy” Annual Review on defining conflicts.

title: Administrative Democracy
text: What institutional mechanisms advance administrative democracy? To be effective, must they be identity-conscious and ends-oriented? Carpenter (2023) points to the “democratic necessity of local political intermediaries, protest campaigns, social organizations, advocacy campaigns, grievance mechanisms, and other agenda-democratizing processes and institutions.” Policies don’t merely create mass politics; they also structure the inevitable and ongoing politics of “filling up the details” and adapting to change (Moynihan and Soss 2014). Neutral processes likely reproduce existing inequalities. Institutions that resist power are often brought about by social movements and are difficult to maintain when the movement ebbs (Wilson 1989).  With most policy still inevitably crafted by bureaucrats, understanding how institutional design makes bureaucratic policymaking responsive to different interests is key, both to understanding the effects of current disruptions and future rebuilding. Redistributive policies will fail if the institutions that “implement” and revise them are responsive to a chorus with an upper-class accent.

title: Administrative Democracy
section: Intermediary institutions as mechanisms of administrative democracy
text:
Intermediary institutions as mechanisms of administrative democracy
Agency policymaking tilts toward business (Yackee and Yackee 2006), whose resources give them access to lawyers, experts, and powerful allies (Libgober and Carpenter 2024; Carpenter et al. 2024; Powell et al. 2023). While centralizing control may shift the venue of conflict from agencies to the White House in some areas, the federal government is vast, and the White House bureaucracy has limited capacity. Where the White House is paying little attention, inequality in the ability to articulate claims and demands in ways that bureaucratic policymakers see as legitimate remains a key problem, and lawyers, experts, and allies will likely continue to matter. As one agency official put it, “some groups don’t speak the King’s English”—intermediary institutions must translate.
On the inside, public advocates and offices of civil rights, environmental justice, and public participation translate internally, increasing responsiveness to these concerns, but they are marginalized within their institutions (Walton 1988; Harrison 2019). The second Trump administration has rapidly moved to dismantle many, but not all, of these offices, likely with long-term effects. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s Office of Public Participation (OPP) persists. While plans to fund public and consumer advocates are on hold, the OPP continues outreach to affected communities and to help lower-resource groups navigate technical proceedings with major consequences for energy markets and infrastructure. Proactive outreach is impactful in theory but is rarely done (Hertel-Fernandez 2025), and research is thin.
From the outside, high-capacity advocacy organizations partner with and thus give voice to low-capacity groups by translating demands into the King’s English. But these partnerships are unequal (Strolovitch 2006; Dwidar 2022). To the extent the White House is able to consolidate authority, the currency of influence may shift from legal and technical legitimacy to access and loyalty, which advocacy groups can only provide under aligned presidents. In contrast, businesses can buy access and pivot loyalties. Protests and petitions can force issues into public discourse and alter the political context of agency decision-making, but they are often dismissed by policymakers who see themselves as expert administrators.
From below, state and local governments are active participants in administrative policymaking, often joining coalitions (related to Lisa’s memo).
Horizontally, congressional offices oversee executive-branch agencies and act as ombudsmen. A large share of congressional staff work on overseeing executive-branch policymaking and implementation as they route constituent problems to the correct agency, translate, and advocate for resolution. Using data from Judge-Lord et al. (2026), Figure 1 shows that congressional offices’ policy work (e.g., oversight investigations, commenting on rules) focuses on first-face agencies, while constituent casework is disproportionately with second-face agencies, dominated by helping constituents navigate immigration bureaucracies.1 But congressional offices are capacity constrained, and the design of the congressional bureaucracy is extremely ad hoc, leading some offices to do much more work to oversee and help their constituents deal with federal agencies than others. Moreover, the congressional bureaucracy is exceptionally White (Jones 2024), and some constituencies, like seniors, are better served than others, like SNAP recipients (Snyder et al. 2025), and work on behalf of business favors campaign donors (Powell et al. 2023). Efforts to control agency communication with members of Congress, centralize decision-making, use federal funds as a bargaining leverage, and reduce transparency may reduce the ability of congressional offices to facilitate agency responsiveness.








Figure 1: Congressional Office Attention to Two Faces of the Administrative State





Some famous intermediary institutions are missing from administrative democracy. Parties craft agendas and then rely on presidents and appointees to see them through. The only party-adjacent actors at the table in bureaucratic policymaking are corporate donors. The party in government is the donor-consultant faction of the party (see Jake and Paul’s memos). Unions, with some exceptions, are narrowly present on issues that directly affect their workplace, often mobilized by employers. National Nurses United is one of the few I engaged more broadly (Ahlquist and Levi 2013). Some broad-based groups, like AARP, are also absent.
While Second Face institutions may have evaded transparency and participation requirements, there is demand for it in the streets and in local politics. For example, municipal cooperation with ICE is now a major flashpoint of local elections. Do second-face agencies demand different accountability institutions?

title: Administrative Democracy
text:
Identity-conscious administrative law
Feinstein (2022) argues that identity-conscious institutional design can improve agency accountability by explicitly elevating certain groups that are disadvantaged by neutral processes. If institutions aim for “equitable and meaningful” participation — to mitigate rather than reproduce structural power — must they explicitly empower race- and class-subjugated communities? We have much more research on identity-targeted benefits and enforcement than identity-conscious participation. Even without elevating certain groups, addressing the identity of participants — about who is lobbying, who they represent, who funded it — could yield more informed decisions (Seifter 2016), incent better internal governance, and strengthen civil society infrastructure (Berger et al. 2026). Despite much discussion about how participation builds legitimacy (Feinstein and Walters 2025), courts pay no attention to the democratic qualities of the policy process or who was excluded when upholding or striking down policy. Proposals to reform public participation are generally framed as neutrally increasing access, assuming that a more open process will lead to more diverse perspectives and higher quality information. What do we know about the limits of identity-neutral participatory institutions, the possibilities of identity-conscious ones, and possible tradeoffs?
Shaping identities and public discourse — disrupting one conventional wisdom and cementing another — is key to how social movements affect policy (Woodly 2015). Policy is shaped by and shapes common sense about what fairness and equal treatment entail. Unlike the first Trump administration, where bureaucrats and policy documents continued to talk about environmental justice and civil rights, efforts to shift the language of policymaking drove nearly all discussion of race, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, minority populations, underserved communities, cultural competency, disparate impact, civil rights, equity, inequality, disability, and tribal consultation to nearly zero in 2025 (e.g., Figure 2).2 How will these changes in policy discourse affect policy substance?

What distinguishes the first and second faces of public administration?
When critics of the administrative state exempt second-face agencies, are they exempting certain institutions, forms of state action, or policy goals? Some distinguish historically constructed policy domains (“domestic affairs” like education, health, and the environment versus “national security” issues like immigration, policing, and foreign affairs). Chertoff and Bulman-Pozen (2025) focus on means (regulation & benefits vs. surveillance & violence). Soss and Weaver (2017) focuses on similar means (coercion, containment, repression, surveillance, regulation, predation, discipline, and violence) and ends (social control of race- and class-subjugated communities). I attempted to classify all federal agencies for each dimension (comments welcome!).
2025 saw 58% fewer rules (Figure 3 (a)) and 56% fewer other documents than the first year of the first Trump administration. This drop in normal policymaking has been somewhat concentrated in first-face agencies (b), not necessarily liberal agencies (c).3 Most significantly, the decrease is almost entirely concentrated in agencies mentioned in more than 10 paragraphs of the Heritage Foundation’s Mandate for Leadership report (d).

title: “Seven Propositions About the Contemporary Democratic Party”
text:
Senate Brain, Lawyer Brain, small status-quo-biased thinking is not limited to the party.
Prominent observers talking about oversight investigations in 2027 regularly say that a committee can only take on 1-3 investigations, so the challenge, they say, is picking what to focus on. This presumes current levels of oversight staff capacity. Even those talking about increasing staffing are thinking on small scales, not proportional to the scale of the problem.
Bureaucrats are the embodiment of formed routine. This causes “not my job” thinking. For example, even the EPA’s Office of Air Resources resisted building climate change into its models of air pollutant formation because climate was somebody else’s job. This was what whole-of-government initiatives around climate and social justice in the Biden administration were intended to fix (growing from G.W. Bush’s faith-based initiatives). Anecdotally, these had interesting effects, forcing conversations in new places. For example, the Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network, an agency stood up in the war on terror populated by lawyers, investigators, and a few economists, launched an initiative to explore how their compliance regulations and enforcement practices may advantage big banks.
The Second Trump administration articulated “whole-of-government” initiatives to support fossil fuels and persecute immigrants, which clearly had massive effects, but their opaque and messy execution through non-traditional channels may make them harder to study.

title: 2025 Changes to U.S. Climate-Relevant Policy
text:
“Energy Emergency” E.O.
To promote oil, gas, biofuels, nuclear, and mining,1 government agencies should:
Sec. 2. Consider using eminent domain & the Defense Production Act to commandeer private lands and companies2
Sec. 3-6. Exempt projects from normal health/safety/cost review

Emergency approvals of public lands leases, pollution permits 
Waive Clean Water Act protections for water quality, wetlands, & coastlines3
Emergency exemptions from Endangered Species Act restrictions on impacts that cause extinctions

Sec. 7. Mobilize the military to build oil and gas infrastructure and aid oil and gas transport and refining
Is it following the Project 2025 playbook?

✘ “Stopping executive overreach. Congress should set policy—not Presidents through pen-and-phone executive orders, and not agencies through regulations and guidance. National emergency declarations should expire absent express congressional authorization within 60 days after the date of the declaration.” - Project 2025

More specifically, “energy” is defined as “crude oil, natural gas, lease condensates, natural gas liquids, refined petroleum products, uranium, coal, biofuels, geothermal heat, the kinetic movement of flowing water, and critical minerals”The Brennan Center has a great summary of Emergency Powers. Interestingly, this Energy Emergency E.O. does not mention that a Governor of a State may petition the President to suspend any part of a Clean Air Act implementation plan or any requirement under Section 110(f) (42 U.S.C. § 7651j), which Carter granted to fossil fuel power plants during regional energy emergencies in the 1970s.As I read it, the emergency powers of the CWA focus emergency restrictions to prevent contamination/poisoning, not to permit it.
